issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 55-year-old Tongan-American man who works as a nanny for a family in suburban Portland, Oregon. He is divorced and lives alone in a small apartment not far from the home where he works. He came to the clinic carrying a PCL-5 score of 65, and in the intake session he sat with his hands folded tightly in his lap, speaking in careful, measured sentences until, at certain moments, he simply stopped mid-sentence and stared at the floor.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rangi was caring for his younger brother Sione, who had been living with him following a serious cancer diagnosis. Rangi had taken on the role of primary caregiver with the quiet, determined devotion that had always characterised his relationships. On the evening that changed everything, Sione suffered a catastrophic medical event - a haemorrhage - while Rangi was in the room. What followed was a period of frantic effort: Rangi pressing his hands against his brother's body trying to slow the bleeding, shouting into the phone for an ambulance, hearing Sione's breathing change into something laboured and wet and then, finally, into nothing. The paramedics arrived too late. Rangi was still kneeling on the floor beside his brother when they came through the door.

In the weeks that followed, Rangi found himself unable to give a coherent account of what had happened, even when he tried to tell his adult daughter over the phone. He would begin the story and then the thread would simply dissolve - words stopped arriving, the sequence collapsed, and he would trail off into silence. He had come to believe this was evidence of something broken in him, proof that he was not the strong, capable man he had always tried to be. What frightened him most was the conviction that he had failed at the one thing that mattered: he had been right there, in the room, and Sione had still died. He was certain that a better man, a stronger man, would have done something differently.

The memories, when they came, were not silent. He could hear the particular quality of Sione's breathing in those final minutes - a sound that now arrived unbidden, playing in his mind with a fidelity that felt almost physical. Along with the sound came grief so acute it was difficult to distinguish from physical pain, a wave that could arrive in the middle of an ordinary afternoon and leave him unable to move for several minutes.

His work as a nanny placed him in close, daily proximity to the children he cared for, and he found that tending to their scraped knees, their small injuries - any moment that required him to look carefully at a child's hands or arms or face in the context of hurt - could stop him cold. The sight of a child's bruised shin, a cut that needed cleaning, any concentrated attention on a body part in distress, carried with it an associative pull he could not fully explain and could not prevent. He began deflecting those moments to the children's parents whenever possible, which the family had noticed and quietly questioned.

When conversations arose at the family dinner table - the parents discussing a news story about loss, a neighbour who had recently been bereaved - Rangi would excuse himself to the kitchen. He had developed a habit of turning on the tap so that the sound of water covered whatever was being said in the next room. Over months, this had created a subtle but perceptible distance between him and the family he worked for, a warmth that had cooled without either side being able to name why.

Perhaps most distressing to Rangi was a creeping sense that he had become somehow less than a person - that he moved through his days as a kind of functional object, present in body but absent in some essential way he could not articulate. He did not share this with many people. He had shared almost nothing with anyone.

What finally brought him to the clinic was his daughter's visit last month. She told him, gently but directly, that she barely recognised him. He sat with that for three weeks before making the call. He came hoping, he said quietly, to find a way to remember Sione without the sound.
